Local facilities required oxygen, fluids, and vasopressors before transfer. Echocardiography showed a severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 25–28% with elevated troponin I. Stool and blood tests confirmed Salmonella infection causing acute gastroenteritis; the source was undercooked eggs in the soup. Salmonella is a common foodborne pathogen in eggs, and killing it requires heating to at least 70°C for 5 minutes. In practice, pouring 100°C boiling water into a room-temperature bowl with raw eggs often drops the temperature below sterilizing levels, failing to kill bacteria. articleSummary: 2026-06-23 – In Quanzhou, Fujian, clinics report a surge in three pediatric infections with summer transmission: varicella (chickenpox), herpangina, and hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD). articleSummary: Across five decades (1976–May 2026), global Ebola spread remains rare: only 28 confirmed epidemic-linked cases outside Africa, with 27 during the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak and a single case linked to the 2026 Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Since 2000, latent exports and their secondary cases amount to 0.17 per 1,000 source-outbreak cases; overall exported cases are 0.81 per 1,000. Ebola transmission is not airborne; infection requires direct contact with infected bodily fluids.

The outbreak is centered in Ituri province around Bunia. About 100 people have recovered; at least 365 patients remain hospitalized or in isolation. The rare Bundibugyo strain is involved, and there is currently no approved vaccine or treatment. Officials have not identified the first infected patient, complicating transmission timeline. Contact tracing covers roughly 55% of known contacts; more than 35,000 exposed individuals still need tracing. Ongoing violence in eastern Congo restricts access to communities and has displaced thousands, hindering control measures. Authorities warn the true scale may exceed reported figures and that the peak of infections may not yet be reached.

articleSummary: As of 2026-06-23, Taiwan reports its first domestically acquired cholera case this year: a woman in her 70s from the southern region with no recent travel. She developed severe diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, and altered consciousness in early June, was hospitalized, and on June 19 laboratory testing confirmed infection with toxigenic Vibrio cholerae; her condition is improving and she has been discharged. Cholera is a notifiable intestinal disease spread mainly through contaminated food and water. Global risk is very high, with about 1 billion people at risk. By April 26, around 79,000 cases and 1,010 deaths were reported worldwide, with outbreaks concentrated in Africa, the Eastern Mediterranean, and Southeast Asia, notably Afghanistan (27,000), the Democratic Republic of Congo (23,000), and Mozambique (7,100). Mortality without treatment exceeds 50% but can fall below 1% with prompt rehydration and care. Preventive guidance includes avoiding raw seafood, ensuring thorough cooking, preventing cross-contamination, drinking boiled water, and refrigerating unused foods.

articleSummary: As of 23 June 2026, Kaohsiung City Health Bureau reported one new imported dengue fever case in Liugui District. The patient is a 24-year-old Peruvian man who arrived in Taiwan on 18 June from Thailand and stayed at a Liugui farm. He developed fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and loss of appetite on 20 June. Dengue NS1 rapid test was positive and laboratory confirmation identified Dengue virus type 2; he is hospitalized. The bureau has launched emergency measures around the residence and activity areas, including vector surveillance, source reduction, and chemical control. They note the domestic dengue in Qianzhen District has exited monitoring, but heavy rainfall and rising mosquito density persist. Public are advised to practice environmental management (inspect, drain, overturn, scrub) and use approved repellents (DEET, Picaridin, IR3535). Returning travelers with fever should report to airport quarantine and seek prompt medical care with travel history (TOCC).

articleSummary: Swine flu (influenza A H1N1) caused a death in Karnataka’s Uttara Kannada district, with the patient dying at a private hospital in Mangaluru after fever began on June 10. He first sought care at a clinic, was admitted in Sirsi taluk, then referred to Mangaluru where labs confirmed swine flu. Contacts and family are under monitoring and advised to wear masks. Swine flu is a viral infection affecting the nose, throat, and lungs. It spreads via airborne droplets from coughing or sneezing and by touching contaminated surfaces. Symptoms typically appear 1–4 days after exposure and can be contagious from one day before to 3–4 days after. Common signs include high fever, cough, sore throat, runny or blocked nose, body aches, headache, and fatigue; severe cases may involve breathing trouble, vomiting, or diarrhea. Treatment includes antivirals, rest, and fluids; most recover in about a week. Prevention focuses on hand hygiene, masking, surface cleaning, avoiding contact with infected people, and seeking care if symptoms worsen.

articleHeadline: Chuyên gia cảnh báo 'sốt xuất huyết không còn thuần túy theo mùa'
articleSummary: Dengue fever in Vietnam is no longer strictly seasonal; climate change and urbanization have shifted transmission to year-round circulation, with spikes during the rainy season. Dengue virus, transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, affects all ages; most infections are mild, but some progress to severe dengue with plasma leakage, shock, hemorrhage, organ failure, and death if untreated. The dangerous phase often occurs as fever subsides (days 3–7) due to rapid plasma leakage and falling platelets. Warning signs include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy, gum or nose bleeding, vomiting blood, black stools, reduced urination, or breathlessness. High-risk groups: pregnant women, infants 1 month–12 months, elderly over 60, and those with chronic diseases. Avoid home IV fluid therapy and NSAIDs like aspirin or ibuprofen; use plain paracetamol under medical guidance. Prevention combines vector control with a tetravalent dengue vaccine for ages 4 and older, reducing infection and hospitalization. Dengue Day is June 15.
notes: 記事は気候変動と都市化によるデング熱の季節性の変化を強調し、重症化の危険性、高リスク集団の特定、予防策（ワクチンと媒介蚊対策）について言及。ベトナムでの持続的な疾病リスク増加が示唆されている。

articleHeadline: How Bad Could the Ebola Outbreak Get? Latest on Testing, Tracing and Vaccines
articleSummary: East Africa Ebola outbreak driven by Bundibugyo virus, centered in Congo near the Uganda border, spreading in crowded displacement camps within an active conflict zone. Early misidentification and limited testing delays mean current case counts likely underestimate true extent. Rapid testing expanded by Congo's national biomedical research institute, with most results processed the same day, but samples remain time-consuming to transport, and lack of electronic records slows data sharing. Public trust is fragile; many are reluctant to seek testing due to isolation fears, misinformation, and cultural rites around death. No therapy or vaccine specific to Bundibugyo exists; WHO emphasizes supportive care. CEPI has committed over $63 million to Bundibugyo vaccine development (four candidates; scale-up underway). Monoclonal MBP-134 shows promise in monkeys and is safe in humans; antivirals like obeldesivir are being planned for post-exposure use. Contact tracing remains critical; Uganda traces almost all contacts, Congo side around 70% recently, with thousands not followed.

articleHeadline: Amazon Research Reveals Hidden Disease Hotspots
articleSummary: Forest‑linked land use and poverty shape hidden disease hotspots in the Brazilian Amazon. From 2015–2019, 1.28 million vector‑borne disease (VBD) cases were reported, with malaria accounting for 75% and dengue 20.1%. Chagas disease tends to co‑occur with malaria, while dengue co‑occurs with American tegumentary leishmaniasis (ATL); visceral leishmaniasis (VL) generally remains isolated. Spatial patterns separate into forest‑linked malaria–Chagas landscapes and agricultural dengue–ATL landscapes. A Western Amazon malaria–Chagas hotspot dominates, with minor hotspots in the northeast where mining and forest cover prevail; a southeast Amazon dengue–ATL hotspot overlaps with malaria–Chagas cold spots. About 97% of dengue–ATL municipalities are livestock‑farming/export‑dominant, while 88% of malaria–Chagas municipalities are peasant agriculture/agroforestry dominated. High deforestation and rural poverty strongly link Chagas–malaria co‑occurrence; large‑scale farming, forest fragmentation, and mining relate to VL and urban Chagas. Datasets and models show socioeconomic/environmental factors explain ~75% of VBD covariance, underscoring need for ecosystemic health strategies.

articleHeadline: Yellow Fever
articleSummary: Yellow fever, transmitted by daytime-biting Aedes aegypti and other mosquitoes (Aedes, Haemagogus), remains a global health security threat. Endemic in 34 African countries and 13 in Central and South America, it causes 29,000–60,000 deaths annually. Incubation is 3–6 days; initial flu-like symptoms may be non-specific, with a minority entering a toxic phase causing liver and kidney damage and up to 50% mortality in 7–10 days. There is no antiviral treatment; care is supportive. A single vaccine dose provides lifelong protection and is recommended for travelers to endemic areas. Prevention includes avoiding bites and vector control; Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes show promise. Notable history includes Panama Canal outbreaks, 1878 Mississippi Valley tragedy, and the 2015–2016 Angola outbreak with a traveler introducing the virus to China—the first imported case there.

articleSummary: {"description":"Leishmaniasis, caused by Leishmania parasites transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies, affects 700,000–1,000,000 people annually, with about 30,000 cases of the most severe form (visceral). articleHeadline: Leprosy
articleSummary: Leprosy (Hansen’s disease), caused by Mycobacterium leprae, affects about 200,000 people worldwide each year. Incubation spans several years to over a decade. Transmission occurs via droplets from the nose or mouth during prolonged close contact; casual contact is not a mode of spread. Early signs are skin changes and nerve involvement; untreated, it can cause irreversible nerve damage, crippling of hands and feet, and may lead to blindness, kidney failure, or disfigurement from skin nodules, with substantial stigma. It is curable with a three-antibiotic regimen for six to twelve months, free since 2000 (Novartis). Prevention centers on early detection, timely treatment, and monitoring close contacts; a single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis is given to contacts. Originating in India, leprosy spread to Europe, where it declined by the 1600s; the bacterium was identified in 1873 (Hansen).

articleSummary: Melioidosis, a tropical infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, is not transmitted person-to-person and poses no spread risk in Russia, according to infectious-disease expert Sergey Voznesensky (RUDN). The bacterium is typically found in soil and water, with endemic areas in Thailand and Southeast Asia. Infection occurs via contact with contaminated soil, inhalation of dust, or consumption of contaminated water or food; rare transmission from animals is noted. Clinical presentations range from asymptomatic to abscesses, pneumonia, and tuberculosis-like illness; high-risk groups include people with immunodeficiency and diabetes. Treated with antibiotics, the disease does not pose local transmission risk in Russia. A tourist who returned from Thailand has been diagnosed with melioidosis in Russia and is hospitalized in serious condition. Russia's Rospotrebnadzor notes two prior imported cases (2017, 2024). Travelers to endemic regions should wear closed footwear, avoid barefoot exposure, refrain from swimming in freshwater, avoid flood zones, and minimize contact with animals.

articleSummary: In Sergipe, Brazil, the Central Public Health Laboratory (Lacen) reports rising sporotrichosis positivity in human samples. articleSummary: Dengue symptoms in adults, children, and babies are described with emphasis on Brazil’s health authorities and Fiocruz data. Common signs include high fever up to 40°C (105°F), eye pain behind the eyes, joint/muscle/bone pain, severe headache, widespread rash, and mild nose or gum bleeding with easy bruising. Alarm signs after fever—intense abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, malaise, and persistent nasal or gum bleeding—warrant immediate medical care. Fiocruz reports the virus travels from the bite to the bloodstream and then to the spleen, liver, and lymphatic tissues during a 4–7 day incubation period, potentially with no symptoms early on. As infection progresses, vascular leakage and plasma loss can occur, leading to dengue hemorrhagic fever, the more severe form. The Ministry of Health cautions against self-medication to avoid masking symptoms, delaying diagnosis, or promoting drug resistance.

In June, Rospotrebnadzor confirmed an imported case in a tourist returning from Thailand; the infection was likely contracted during excursions, including an elephant farm. Burkholderia pseudomallei, the causative bacterium, resides in soil and in endemic regions worldwide. Transmission occurs through direct skin contact with contaminated soil, inhalation of the organism, ingestion of contaminated food or water, or contact with infected animals. Symptoms include high fever, muscle and chest pain, coughing with purulent sputum mixed with blood, diarrhea, and abscesses at various sites. The disease circulates in Southeast Asia, Africa, Central and South America, the Caribbean, and Oceania, with tourism-relevant countries such as Vietnam, China, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, Thailand, India, Maldives, Sri Lanka, Nepal, among others.

articleSummary: During the Jiangnan plum rain season, damp indoor spaces foster pathogenic molds. In Ningbo, a couple developed fever and cough; doctors diagnosed aspergillosis pneumonia after mold spores from a damp living room wall cavity entered the lungs. The four common indoor molds cited are Penicillium, Aspergillus, Chaetomium, and Cladosporium, which can cling to curtains, carpets, and tile seams, potentially causing infection in those with underlying illness or weakened immunity. Another risk is Legionella from unclean air-conditioner condensate pans and filters; studies found 88% of home AC units exceeded bacterial standards, enabling aerosolized Legionella. Food safety deteriorates too: fried rice/leftovers can harbor Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, and Escherichia coli; the recommended safe window is two hours at room temperature, one hour if above 35°C. Milk tea and other beverages with toppings quickly multiply bacteria after 1–2 hours. Cleaning ACs, separating raw/cooked foods, and thorough reheating are advised.

articleSummary: A Russian tourist returning from Thailand was diagnosed with melioidosis, a severe infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. Melioidosis is highly lethal in septic forms; case fatality rates range from 15–40% and can reach 80% with septicemia. The disease occurs in tropical/subtropical regions, notably Thailand, Vietnam, and India. The patient presented with fever, chills, headache, cough, chest pain, lymphadenitis, and diarrhea, with the lungs, pleura, kidneys, and liver commonly affected. It can be acute, subacute, or chronic and may begin with nonspecific symptoms; septicemia can rapidly cause abscess-forming pneumonia or empyema. Risk factors include age over 45, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease, alcoholism, cancer, and prolonged steroid use. Transmission is via contaminated water or food, inhalation, or skin contact; reservoirs include rodents and domestic/wild animals. The patient was hospitalized in Russia in severe condition after Thailand visits, including an elephant farm; there is no effective vaccine.

articleSummary: Ranavirus, a double-stranded DNA virus in the Iridoviridae family, poses a severe threat to amphibians in Brazil and beyond. In Brazil, the American bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana) was introduced for meat production; after farms closed, many escaped and facilitated ranavirus spread to native, highly sensitive amphibian populations. The virus, which may be enveloped or non-enveloped, causes infected frogs to stop feeding, have difficulty swimming, and develop skin hemorrhages with swelling, including hemorrhages in the spleen, liver, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract. There is no treatment or vaccine, and the disease is not zoonotic. Ecological consequences include potential rises in mosquito populations, increasing transmission risk for dengue, yellow fever, Zika, chikungunya, and malaria. The piece underscores how climate change, pollution, and habitat loss compound amphibian declines and the broader ecosystem impacts of pathogen introductions.

articleSummary: Idaf launched surveillance in Tarauacá's interior, Acre, after local reports of atypical cattle mortality. Field teams along a rural ramal of the Tarauacá-Cruzeiro do Sul road found at least one animal with severe neurological signs (marked difficulty walking and unsteady gait). Euthanasia and necropsy were conducted; an encephalon sample was sent for laboratory rabies testing in herbivores, while investigators noted toxic plants and bones on pasture, factors under investigation. The initial rabies hypothesis weakens given the herd was current with anti-rabies vaccination and no reported hematophagous bat (Desmodus rotundus) attacks. Idaf follows the PNCRH guidelines: bat cave/registers, sanitary education, and targeted monitoring in high-risk microregions. Concurrently, epidemiological lines explore accidental ingestion of native poisonous plants and clostridial diseases (including symptomatic carbuncle/anthrax and botulism). A national shortage of clostridial vaccines limits preventive immunization; surveillance remains active in Vale do Juruá until lab results are available. Producers reporting signs should notify Idaf.
